smRotationNotEnabled.^description: {$COUNT} secret(s) do not have automatic rotation enabled (RotationEnabled is false or unset). A static credential that never changes stays valid indefinitely once leaked, so any exposure through a log, a code repository or a compromised host grants an attacker unbounded access. Automatic rotation caps that exposure window to the rotation interval. Secrets owned by another AWS service (OwningService set, e.g. rds!...) are reported as not-applicable because the owning service controls their rotation.
smRotationNotEnabled.shortDesc: Enable automatic rotation on every secret

smRotationOverdue.^description: {$COUNT} secret(s) have rotation enabled but have not rotated within their own configured interval — LastRotatedDate is older than RotationRules.AutomaticallyAfterDays, or rotation was turned on and has never run at all. This almost always means the rotation function is failing silently, so the operator believes the credential is rotating when it is in fact as stale as an unrotated secret.
smRotationOverdue.shortDesc: Investigate the failing rotation and rotate the secret now

smNotEncryptedWithCMK.^description: {$COUNT} secret(s) are encrypted with the AWS-managed key aws/secretsmanager rather than a customer-managed KMS key (KmsKeyId is omitted or resolves to the aws/secretsmanager alias). The AWS-managed key cannot carry a key policy, so access to the secret material cannot be constrained or revoked at the key layer, and its rotation and grants are not under your control.
smNotEncryptedWithCMK.shortDesc: Encrypt secrets with a customer-managed KMS key

smNotUsedRecently.^description: {$COUNT} secret(s) have not been retrieved in this region for more than 90 days (LastAccessedDate is older than 90 days, or the secret has never been retrieved and is itself older than 90 days). An unused secret is still a live credential and still billed monthly, so it is either an orphan that should be deleted or a credential nobody is monitoring.
smNotUsedRecently.shortDesc: Review and delete secrets that are no longer retrieved

smResourcePolicyPublicAccess.^description: {$COUNT} secret(s) have a resource policy with an Allow statement whose Principal is "*" and which carries no scoping Condition (aws:PrincipalOrgID, aws:SourceAccount, aws:SourceArn, aws:PrincipalArn or equivalent). Combined with a permissive IAM policy this can expose the secret value to principals outside the account, which is the highest-impact misconfiguration possible on a secret store.
smResourcePolicyPublicAccess.shortDesc: Remove or constrain wildcard-principal statements on the secret policy

smResourcePolicyCrossAccount.^description: {$COUNT} secret(s) grant access to a principal in another AWS account without an organisation- or ARN-scoping Condition (aws:PrincipalOrgID, aws:PrincipalOrgPaths, aws:PrincipalArn, aws:SourceArn or a VPC-endpoint condition). Account-level grants stay in force after the trusted account changes hands or its roles are recreated, so the grant should be narrowed to the exact principal or bounded by your organisation ID.
smResourcePolicyCrossAccount.shortDesc: Scope cross-account grants with a PrincipalOrgID or PrincipalArn condition

smReplicationNotConfigured.^description: {$COUNT} secret(s) exist in a single region with no replica (ReplicationStatus is empty). A workload that fails over to another region cannot read a secret that only exists in the failed region, so the secret becomes a single-region dependency in an otherwise multi-region recovery plan. This is advisory for single-region workloads.
smReplicationNotConfigured.shortDesc: Replicate secrets needed by multi-region workloads

smPendingDeletion.^description: {$COUNT} secret(s) are scheduled for deletion (DeletedDate is set). While inside the recovery window the secret value cannot be retrieved, so any workload still calling GetSecretValue is already failing; once the window closes the material is unrecoverable. Confirm the deletion was intended, or restore the secret before the window expires.
smPendingDeletion.shortDesc: Confirm the scheduled deletion or restore the secret

smNoDescription.^description: {$COUNT} secret(s) have an empty or unset Description. Without a description an operator inspecting the account cannot tell what the secret protects or who owns it, which is what turns unused secrets into permanent orphans nobody dares delete.
smNoDescription.shortDesc: Describe every secret so its owner and purpose are discoverable

smNoTags.^description: {$COUNT} secret(s) have no tags. Tags are the only mechanism for attributing the per-secret monthly charge to a cost centre and for writing tag-based IAM conditions (secretsmanager:ResourceTag), so untagged secrets are both unattributable and harder to authorise at scale.
smNoTags.shortDesc: Apply an ownership and environment tag to every secret

smVersionsExcessive.^description: {$COUNT} secret(s) retain more than 10 non-current versions (versions in VersionIdsToStages that do not carry the AWSCURRENT stage). Every labelled version is retained indefinitely, so a rotation function that attaches a custom staging label on each run accumulates versions without bound; unlabelled versions are pruned automatically once there are more than 100.
smVersionsExcessive.shortDesc: Stop attaching custom staging labels on every rotation

smNoVersionStages.^description: {$COUNT} secret(s) have no version carrying the AWSCURRENT staging label. GetSecretValue defaults to AWSCURRENT, so every consumer of the secret fails until the label is moved onto a version. This is normally the aftermath of a rotation that was interrupted between creating AWSPENDING and promoting it.
smNoVersionStages.shortDesc: Move the AWSCURRENT label onto a valid secret version

smRotationLambdaMissing.^description: {$COUNT} secret(s) have RotationEnabled=True but no RotationLambdaARN, and are not using managed rotation or managed external rotation. Secrets Manager has nothing to invoke, so every scheduled rotation fails while the console still reports rotation as turned on — the worst of both states.
smRotationLambdaMissing.shortDesc: Attach a rotation function or turn rotation off

smLastChangedOld.^description: {$COUNT} secret(s) have not been modified in over 365 days (LastChangedDate) and have no rotation configured. The credential they hold has therefore been valid for more than a year, so every person and system that has ever seen it still holds a working key — including former staff and decommissioned hosts.
smLastChangedOld.shortDesc: Rotate long-lived static secrets at least annually

smAutoRotationScheduleInvalid.^description: {$COUNT} secret(s) have RotationRules but no ScheduleExpression, so the rotation schedule is implicit in AutomaticallyAfterDays alone. Without a cron() or rate() expression you cannot pin rotation to a maintenance window or set a Duration, which means rotation can fire in the middle of peak traffic and break consumers that cache the credential.
smAutoRotationScheduleInvalid.shortDesc: Define a ScheduleExpression so rotation lands in a maintenance window
